about: Learning to cook in the holidays

lines.text: Last June, my mother announced that I would cook dinner once a week.
I had never made anything more difficult than instant noodles, so I was
nervous. My first attempt was fried rice, which sound easy but was not.
lines.note: Tense: the story is in the past, so it is 'sounded'.

lines.text: I added too many soy sauce, and the rice turned dark and salty.
lines.note: 'Much' goes with things you cannot count, like soy sauce.

lines.text: My brother ate it anyway, although he drank three glass of water afterwards.
The following week, I watched my grandmother closely as she prepared chicken curry.
She never measures anything, but each dish she makes taste exactly the same.
lines.note: Agreement: 'each dish' is singular, so it is 'tastes'.

lines.text: That day, she let I stir the pot while she explained each step slowly.
By the end of the holidays, I could prepared four dishes without help.
lines.note: Verb form: after 'could' the verb stays plain — 'prepare'.

lines.text: Cooking has also made me more grateful to the meals my parents make
lines.note: Preposition: we are grateful 'for' a thing.

lines.text: after a long day at work. I am still a slowly cook, but
lines.note: Word form: 'cook' is a noun here, so it takes the adjective 'slow'.

lines.text: nobody at our table reaches for the water jug any more.
